strengths: Addresses a practical and well-motivated problem of generating videos with controlled actor-target interactions
Intuitive and implementable approach using segmentation masks and a novel cross-attention loss to guide video generation
Comprehensive evaluation including multiple quantitative metrics (Contact Score, VBench quality measures), user studies, and ablation studies
Demonstrates real applications in video content creation and zero-shot 3D HOI motion synthesis
Clear presentation and reasonable reproducibility with implementation details in appendix
Curated dataset with segmentation annotations for target-aware learning with promise to release
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: Core contribution is relatively incremental - adding mask conditioning and a straightforward cross-attention loss to existing diffusion models, building on well-established attention-based guidance techniques
Critically small training dataset of only 50 images raises serious questions about generalization and model robustness; insufficient scale for deep generative model training

Incomplete experimental evaluation: Missing statistical significance testing, limited baseline comparisons (only CogVideoX variants and drag-based methods), unaddressed video quality trade-off shown in Table 1
Evaluation methodology concerns: Contact Score based on proximity detection may not capture semantic correctness; user study details sparse (participant counts and methodology not fully specified)
Limited scope with narrow generalization: All qualitative results from similar indoor scenes; no systematic evaluation of complex scenes, diverse objects, multiple actors, or failure case analysis
Technical justification gaps: Block selection (5-23) appears ad-hoc without ablation; no sensitivity analysis for mask quality; temporal consistency not explicitly analyzed
Real-world applicability limited: Applications require additional complex components (3D insertion, physics simulation); no end-to-end quality evaluation
Reproducibility gaps: Dataset composition vague ('newly curated'), training vs. evaluation prompt strategy unclear, exact computational costs not specified, notation inconsistencies

strengths: Well-motivated problem addressing a real limitation of video diffusion models in accurately generating target-aware interactions
Comprehensive evaluation methodology including contact detection metrics, video quality measures, qualitative comparisons, and user studies
Thorough ablation studies examining the contribution of different components (transformer blocks, attention regions, loss weights)
Practical demonstrations of two downstream applications: video content creation and zero-shot 3D HOI motion synthesis
Curated dataset contribution for target-aware human-object interaction scenarios
weaknesses: Severely limited dataset with only 50 training images, raising fundamental questions about generalization and reproducibility
Marginal empirical improvements with no statistical significance testing (e.g., 0.986 vs 0.984 contact score, identical video quality metrics of 0.812)
Limited technical novelty - primarily applies straightforward combinations of existing techniques (mask inputs + attention loss) without fundamental innovation
Weak baseline comparisons with no comparison to simpler alternatives like mask-based inpainting and insufficient coverage of recent controllable video generation methods
Reproducibility concerns with no confirmed code/dataset release, small dataset size, and underspecified dataset curation procedures
Limited scope and unclear generalization: only demonstrated on human-object interactions in controlled indoor scenes with minimal evidence beyond these settings
Evaluation methodology lacks statistical significance testing, unclear user study sample sizes for some experiments, and relies on potentially unreliable hand detection for contact scoring
Empirical evidence insufficient to support claims of improvement: identical video quality scores across methods and modest contact score gains within noise margins

strengths: Well-motivated problem addressing accurate actor-target interactions in video generation, which is practically important and insufficiently addressed by prior methods
Comprehensive evaluation combining quantitative metrics, qualitative comparisons, ablation studies, and user studies (50+ participants) across multiple dimensions
Thoughtful technical design with selective application of cross-attention loss to transformer blocks and identification of semantically-relevant regions for effective guidance
Practical downstream applications demonstrating utility for video content creation and 3D HOI motion synthesis
Good experimental methodology with meaningful baselines (drag-based editing) and control metrics (contact score, video quality metrics)
Reproducibility-focused with implementation details in appendix and promise to release code and curated dataset
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: core contribution is straightforward application of well-established techniques (mask conditioning, attention-based guidance) to video diffusion with relatively incremental modifications to CogVideoX
Selection of transformer blocks (5-23) for cross-attention loss appears empirically determined without principled justification; method shows sensitivity to λ_attn weight requiring tuning

Weak baseline selection: primarily compares against unmodified CogVideoX and drag-based methods rather than other recent controllable generation approaches specifically designed for interaction control

Generalization concerns: limited to controlled indoor scenes with relatively small curated dataset (1,290 images); unclear how method performs on outdoor scenes, complex multi-actor scenarios, or diverse object categories
Evaluation limitations: contact score relies on hand detection quality; borrowed video metrics not interaction-specific; modest user study scale (~10 videos per method); no failure case analysis
Technical gaps: handling of target occlusion during generation not discussed; computational overhead compared to baselines not reported; custom dataset construction process incompletely detailed
Zero-shot 3D HOI application feels disconnected from main contribution with only qualitative results; unclear if improvements come from target-aware model or better pose inputs to physics simulator
Brief limitations section without thorough discussion of failure modes, and some assumptions (availability of segmentation masks) limit practical applicability

strengths: Well-motivated and practical problem addressing a genuine gap in controllable video generation
Comprehensive experimental evaluation including quantitative metrics (Contact Score, VBench), two user studies, extensive ablations, and diverse qualitative results
Thoughtful engineering with selective cross-attention loss applied to relevant attention regions and transformer blocks
Practical downstream applications (3D HOI motion synthesis, video content creation) demonstrating real utility
Robustness analysis showing resilience to noisy captions, mask quality variations, and different mask shapes
Clear presentation with well-structured figures and honest discussion of limitations
Curated benchmark dataset contribution for target-aware video generation evaluation
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty - primarily applies existing techniques (cross-attention loss, token conditioning) to a new problem rather than introducing fundamental innovations
Incomplete baseline comparisons - mostly compares against CogVideoX and in-house method; drag-based editing methods shown only qualitatively despite claims of superiority

Quantitative metric limitations - Contact Score depends on hand detection (generalizes poorly), thresholds appear arbitrary, doesn't measure semantic correctness of interactions, and VBench may not capture interaction quality
Modest evaluation scale - dataset of ~12,000 videos, user study with 50 participants and 10 videos per method, no statistical significance testing or inter-rater reliability reported

Critical unresolved limitations - fails when single mask covers multiple objects, cannot handle temporal target switching, requires static target specification throughout video, and contact metrics don't work for non-human agents
Scalability concerns - requires additional channel per target (quadratic scaling for multiple targets), proposed multi-target solution appears impractical
Insufficient failure analysis - limited systematic investigation of when and why method fails beyond showing example failures
Reproducibility issues - dataset availability unclear, no code release mentioned, exact LLM prompts not fully specified, design choices lack justification
Method specificity - selective attention loss application based on empirical observations may not generalize beyond this task; extensive tuning limits applicability

strengths: Well-motivated problem with practical applications in controllable video generation
Clear technical approach with intuitive [TGT] token mechanism and selective cross-attention loss
Comprehensive ablation studies examining loss weights, selective blocks, mask quality, and attention modulation
Reasonable visual results demonstrating target-aware interactions across diverse scenarios
Multiple downstream applications (3D HOI synthesis, video navigation) showing broader utility
Thorough experimental analysis including quantitative metrics, user studies, and qualitative comparisons
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: Core contribution is relatively incremental—adding a token and cross-attention loss to existing I2V model; cross-attention manipulation for control is well-established
Very small training dataset (80 manually annotated images, ~400 training videos) raises serious concerns about generalization and scalability
Manual dataset curation (mask annotation, caption refinement) is not scalable and limits reproducibility
Insufficient baseline comparisons: Only compared against vanilla CogVideoX and drag-based methods; missing comparisons with other controllable/conditional video generation approaches
Weak evaluation metrics: Contact Score relies on hand detection from pre-trained models rather than ground truth; metric fails for non-human interactions
Limited quantitative improvements: Contact Scores in Table 1 show only marginal differences (0.646-0.747) without statistical significance testing
Fundamental scalability limitation: Architecture requires adding channels per target, which scales poorly for many targets
Method limited to single fixed target per video with temporal switching not addressed; struggles with multiple objects of same type
Ad-hoc design choices: [TGT] token mechanism lacks justification; selective loss block selection (5-23) driven by GPU constraints rather than principled analysis
Generalization concerns: Model requires fine-tuning on small task-specific dataset; performance degrades on complex/outdoor scenes; assumes static camera and fixed target throughout video
Reproducibility issues: Dependent on CogVideoX accessibility; manual curation process incompletely documented; no mention of code/dataset release
Insufficient failure analysis and missing ablations: No sensitivity analysis for prompt quality, computational cost not reported, failure modes briefly discussed

strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem formulation addressing an important gap in controllable video generation
Technically sound approach with clever use of [TGT] tokens and selective cross-attention loss, well-justified design choices
Comprehensive and rigorous evaluation including custom benchmark, multiple metrics (Contact Score, Interaction Score, VBench), user studies (50 participants), and extensive ablations
Demonstrated strong generalization: despite training only on human interactions, generalizes to non-human agents, diverse scenarios (indoor/outdoor, simple/complex), and different camera angles
Practical utility demonstrated through two downstream applications: zero-shot 3D HOI synthesis and long-term video generation
Thorough experimental analysis with honest discussion of limitations, failure modes, and ablation studies examining robustness to noisy captions and mask quality
Excellent presentation with clear writing, well-organized structure, effective visualizations, and detailed implementation details supporting reproducibility
weaknesses: Limited novelty in individual technical components: [TGT] tokens and cross-attention loss are relatively straightforward; primary contribution is in their combination rather than fundamental innovation
Method requires input segmentation masks which may not always be available or accurate; Table 7 shows performance degradation with automatically generated masks (0.896 → 0.864 Contact Score)
Evaluation dataset is relatively small (80 images, 240 total videos) sourced from specific domains (BEHAVE, Ego-ExoD), potentially limiting generalizability claims for a top-tier venue

Significant scalability concerns: architecture requires additional channel per target, making it impractical for multi-target scenarios; acknowledged in C.5 but no solution provided; single-mask constraint causes failure in Figure 24
Contact Score metric limitations: relies on contact detector designed for human-hand interactions, acknowledged to fail for non-human scenarios, potentially underestimating success in edge cases
Motion quality analysis is limited; while Contact Score evaluates interaction accuracy, motion realism is less thoroughly examined; failure cases (Figures 24-25) reveal temporal consistency issues

Limited comparative analysis: comparison with other controllable video generation methods is sparse; Attention Modulation baseline appears to be a variant of their approach rather than independent method
Temporal limitations: all demonstrations use short videos (~2 seconds); behavior on longer-duration videos unclear; temporal target switching left as future work
